source.title: fMRI predictors based on language models of increasing complexity recover brain left lateralization

record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream predictability using fMRI brain-response prediction and NLP performance measures, rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss.
record.gate_note: The study measures fMRI prediction performance across language-model sizes and its association with perplexity and HellaSwag. It does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss, token or compute scaling, or a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Random-vector, random-embedding and GloVe baselines are mentioned but are not cataloged because they do not test the downstream-predictability version.
record.test_reason: The study treats fMRI encoding performance, a linear-probe fit of model activations to brain data, as a downstream measure. It reports how this measure scales with log parameter count across 28 English models, and also 10 Chinese and 4 French models. It also relates the measure to Wikitext-2 perplexity, which is close to held-out LM loss, and to HellaSwag. This is a new setting for V6, so T3 rather than T2. Whether brain-encoding fit counts as a 'downstream task' is debatable; researchers may prefer to treat it as a related construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors' primary claims are two: brain score rises linearly with log parameter count, replicating Antonello et al. (2024) across three languages and including Mamba; and a left-hemisphere advantage emerges and grows with model size. They note that the size relationship breaks down above 3B parameters, while NLP performance measures still predict brain score there.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates neural-network activations as predictors of fMRI time courses; it does not fit or test held-out pretraining-loss scaling laws or compute-optimal training allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The parameter-count relationship differs in the subset above 3B parameters; the study also reports results across English, Chinese and French, different model families, whole-brain versus reliable-voxel analyses, and different NLP performance measures.

fits_no_version.finding: The left-minus-right hemisphere difference in brain score increases with log parameter count (r=0.89, p=1.8e−10). This relationship is flat in untrained models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Brain-encoding lateralization grows with LM scale; this is not a scaling-law version.

record.problems: The main English analysis uses a group-average subject; individual-level analyses cover only five participants. The parameter-count relationship is not significant for the ten largest models. The French and Chinese results are presented in figures and summarized in text without numerical association statistics.
record.rows_left_out: Left-right asymmetry, region-of-interest, training-stage, and individual-participant findings are not extracted because they do not measure the downstream-predictability outcome in V6. Random-vector, random-embedding and GloVe baseline results are also left out because they do not test a claim version.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute is not fitted. Perplexity is used only as a predictor of brain score.
No extrapolation from small runs to large runs.
There is no controlled comparison of model shape at fixed parameter count. Family differences (OPT vs Mistral, Mamba lower) are confounded with training data.
Pretraining loss scaling in other modalities or regimes is not tested.
Standard NLP downstream tasks are not tested against scale here. Scaling with training tokens appears only through the Pythia checkpoint figure, with no statistic.
Fitting choices for loss exponents are not examined. The reported bend above 3B parameters concerns brain score, not loss.

missing.what: Whole-brain analysis for the 10 largest models: parameter count r=0.21, p=0.56; perplexity r=0.86, p=1.4e−3; HellaSwag r=0.90, p=3.8e−4. Full-set whole-brain correlations: perplexity r=0.91, HellaSwag r=0.95.
Individual-subject whole-brain brain score versus log parameter count, 9 models: r = 0.88, 0.84, 0.83, 0.87 and 0.96, all p<0.01.
Pythia-6.9B brain score improves over training checkpoints up to 300B tokens. This is figure only.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's tranche is changed from T2 to T3 because the fMRI encoding setting is new rather than a different method for the same measure. The relationship is linear in log parameters, a scaling-law shape, but no power-law exponent is fitted. Inclusion under V6 depends on accepting brain-encoding fit as a downstream task.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens or compute.
Whether small-run fits predict much larger runs' held-out pretraining losses.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their scaling with compute.
Effect of architecture shape at fixed parameter count on pretraining loss.
Power-law behavior of loss across modalities or training regimes. The study examines multiple languages, but evaluates fMRI prediction rather than loss scaling in other modalities or regimes.
Downstream tasks other than the study's fMRI prediction measure and its reported NLP metrics; causal or quantitative prediction of downstream performance from held-out pretraining loss.
Dependence of pretraining-loss exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices and setup; the reported bend concerns brain-prediction performance, not pretraining loss.

tranche.reason: The study tests V6 in fMRI encoding, extending the result to another dataset, three languages and additional model families. It does not measure pretraining-loss power laws or compute-optimal allocation.

source_check.notes: Brain scores use ridge regression on participant-averaged fMRI data and the best correlation across layers for each voxel. These are cross-model associations, not prospective extrapolation tests; the authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased.
